note.text: Cameroon has diverse soils. School groupings include strongly weathered ferrallitic soils across much of the humid south, ferruginous tropical soils in more seasonal northern settings, volcanic-derived soils in uplands and young alluvial deposits on floodplains. Hydromorphic soils reflect prolonged wetness; clay-rich cracking soils also occur in northern plains. These categories overlap different classification traditions and do not map perfectly onto modern WRB names. Climate, parent material, relief, organisms, drainage and time interact. A broad label does not establish fertility, crop suitability or erosion resistance at every site.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to connect broad soil groups to formation and landscape position while evaluating suitability from observed properties. Builds on: soil components, profiles and Cameroon’s climate and vegetation. Leads to: later resource management and evidence-based land-use decisions.

sections.heading: Follow the local example or model
sections.text: Compare a southern weathered plateau, a western volcanic upland and a seasonally wet river plain. Local research around Bambouto and Bokito shows differences within the same broad landscape. Volcanic-derived soils can have favourable properties but still erode on exposed slopes; flood deposits can supply material while flood risk remains. The appropriate assessment combines depth, texture, acidity, nutrients, drainage and slope rather than choosing from colour or regional name alone.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Describe origin and observed properties, then explain an opportunity and a limitation. Distinguish parent-material terms from wetness terms. Do not assume every alluvial or volcanic soil is equally fertile, or every red soil is infertile. This is classroom evaluation, not a fertiliser prescription or permission to alter drainage; local survey and agronomic evidence are needed.

cards.idea: Distinguish the features before applying them.
example: ferrallitic grouping: strongly weathered soils common in humid tropical settings.
ferruginous tropical grouping: a traditional grouping associated with more seasonal tropical weathering.
volcanic-derived soil: soil developed from volcanic parent material with properties varying by development and site.
alluvial material: sediment deposited by rivers and forming part of young floodplain soils.
hydromorphic condition: soil development influenced by prolonged saturation.
shrink-swell clay soil: a clay-rich soil showing marked contraction on drying and expansion on wetting.

pick.q: A humid southern site has a deeply weathered, leached soil. A crop is being considered.
pick.r: Assess acidity and available nutrients as well as texture before choosing management.
w: Assume red colour guarantees every nutrient is abundant.
Ignore soil tests because every forest soil is permanently fertile.
Use a universal chemical dose without local evidence.
e: Colour does not establish all nutrient supplies.
Forest biomass is not proof of a rich enduring soil nutrient store.
No rate can be inferred from a broad soil label alone.
pick.y: Soil suitability requires observed properties and the crop’s requirements.

pick.q: A floodplain site has recent alluvial deposits and seasonal waterlogging.
pick.r: Examine flooding and drainage alongside the deposited material.
w: Treat recent deposits as a guarantee of year-round safe access.
Assume every alluvial site is chemically identical.
Classify the site as hard bedrock solely because it is low.
e: Flood and drainage risk remain relevant.
Deposited materials and later development vary.
Low position does not imply coherent bedrock at the surface.
pick.y: Potential benefits of deposition must be weighed against water conditions.

pick.q: An upland soil is developed from volcanic material on a steep exposed slope.
pick.r: Assess erosion exposure and measured soil properties despite potentially favourable parent material.
w: Assume volcanic origin cancels all slope erosion.
Infer identical fertility at every volcanic site.
Remove cover because all upland soils are immune to runoff.
e: Parent material does not remove the effect of slope and cover.
Age, weathering, drainage and organic matter vary.
Exposure can increase erosion risk.
pick.y: Volcanic origin is relevant but does not determine every property or safe use.

pick.q: A valley soil remains saturated for a long period.
pick.r: Consider oxygen availability and hydromorphic conditions before selecting land use.
w: Assume more saturation always gives roots more oxygen.
Ignore water-table depth because only colour matters.
Conclude that saturation proves no soil organisms exist anywhere.
e: Water-filled pores can restrict air supply.
Drainage and saturation need direct evidence.
Wet conditions change communities and processes rather than proving universal absence of life.
pick.y: Water regime affects soil processes and rooting conditions.
